[The Start of Current Turn Question]
Is is possible to dispute IRS underpayment penalties?
[The End of Current Turn Question]

[The Start of Reference Answer]
Yes, it is possible to dispute IRS underpayment penalties. Nervelessness if the underpayment penalty is due to an honest mistake, it is still applicable. The likelihood of successfully disputing such a penalty may be low, but it is within your rights to appeal. Additionally, if your income is not evenly distributed throughout the year, you may be able to lower or eliminate the penalty by figuring your underpayment using the annualized income installment method and submitting a Schedule AI and Form 2210. The underpayment penalty is simply interest on late payments, regardless of whether they are willful or not. Any perception of willfulness would result in additional penalties.
[The End of Reference Answer]

[The Start of Assistant's Answer]
The documents do not establish whether or how you can formally dispute an IRS underpayment penalty. They do clarify that an “honest mistake” does not by itself mean the penalty is inapplicable: the underpayment penalty is described as interest on late payments, regardless of willfulness; willful conduct may lead to additional penalties. [S1][S4]

If you believe a tax preparer caused the problem, the documents recommend carefully reading the IRS letter and consulting a different preparer with EA or CPA credentials. They also describe complaints and possible damages against a preparer, but do not establish that these actions cancel the IRS penalty. [S2][S3]
[The End of Assistant's Answer]

[The Start of Document]

"The underpayment ""penalty"" is just interest on the late payments--willful or not has nothing to do with it.  When they feel it's willful there will be additional penalties."

d on a specific IRS form which you would sign). If your accountant is lying to you, then you should use form 14157 to complain about him to the IRS. Read carefully the letter you've got from the IRS.

 See here for more details about what reporting you were supposed to do, depending on your situation. I suggest you go to a (different) tax preparer, make sure he is in fact licensed (I.e.: has EA or CPA credentials), and ask him to sort it out. If indeed the original preparer didn't file your return, you can also (in addition to the form 14157) file a complaint with your State regulatory agency that oversees tax preparers, if there's such. If the original preparer made a mistake, it is your right to sue for damages (including the costs of sorting it out, and penalties that you might have incurred due to that mistake).
